Plus Demuth and Chauvin, the P-AI-oneer Press, and a very special newspaper column in today's Flyover news roundup.

5:29 PM CDT on October 27, 2026

Welcome back to The Flyover, your daily digest of important, overlooked, and/or interesting Minnesota news stories.

Sign up for The Flyover newsletter

In a report that will truly shock NextDoor posters across the metro area, Zutobi has selected Minneapolis as the best city for parking in the U.S. And the runner-up? St. Paul.

What the hell is Zutobi? Its primary biz seems to be offering online driver’s test prep, but it's also one of those sites that hires publicists to pitch clickbait lists to gullible hacks like me.

And, well, sometimes (especially when I know it’ll annoy the easily annoyed) I can’t resist sharing these very scientific and definitive reports. As someone who recently became Someone Who Doesn’t Even Own a Car, this one seemed a gimme.

My theory on why people think parking sucks here is the same as my general theory beyond every complaint about the Twin Cities: There are simply more people here than there were 30 years ago.

You could deposit your car pretty much anywhere in 1996 because you lived in an urban area that had emptied itself out. And so Twin Citians came to believe that they have a god-given right to park directly in front of their home and/or destination for free.

So next time you’re having a hard time finding a spot, just be grateful that you don’t live in… literally any other American city.

I don’t need to tell Racket readers this, but if Republicans win statewide races because of “fraud” or “crime” or “affordability” or some other buzzy campaign koan, they’ll do all sorts of evil shit that no one actually wants. Some of it we might not even have thought of.

Take “pardoning Derek Chauvin.” Not an issue I’d considered, since I was more worried about gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth rolling back social programs and abortion protections. Then I read this story from Michelle Griffith at the Minnesota Reformer.

When Demuth was asked if she would pardon George Floyd’s convicted murderer, her running mate, Ryan Wilson, popped in to demand that rival Amy Klobuchar pledge not to pardon “any child rapist ever.” He was referencing Tou Lue Vang, who received a pardon this year after serving 20 years of his sexual assault sentence. (FWIW Klobuchar, while distancing herself from politically poisonous Gov. Tim Walz, has said she "would have clearly not pardoned a sex offender.")

Demuth then deflected the question. “Are there any more questions to do with the fraud?” she asked.

Yes, I have one: Please produce a shred of evidence supporting your inflated $9 billion fraud figure, which former U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson invented last December.

Imagine pernicious bots saying nice things about Bon Jovi under the byline of Pioneer Press critic Ross Raihala. Is that really the future you want to leave your children?

With the assistance of their union, the Minnesota Newspaper & Communications Guild, PiPress employees are trying to secure basic protections regarding the use of AI. What they want: No use of AI slop under a writer’s byline or without an editor’s review, no deepfakes, and no AI-related layoffs. Pretty basic shit.

The paper’s owner, MediaNews Group, has not agreed to these protections because MediaNews Group is a bad boss. (Note: There are no good bosses, only harmless ones who stay out your way and let you do your work.) As Racket's Jay Boller reported in 2023, the Alden Capital subsidiary has starved the PiPress budget and eliminated 80% of its employees over the past nine years.

Anyway, sign this letter in support of the union’s demands; it’s more than halfway to its goal of 400 signatures.

I am not a regular reader of the Winona Post, and so I don't know if “Once Upon a Peanut Butter Parfait,” by Dr. Robert Hicks, columnist, is indicative of his work, but this column is… something else.

“A young man in tight jeans and free-flowing Fabio Lorenzo-styled 1990s hair” walks into a Dairy Queen, and then…" well, let Dr. Robert Hicks tell you himself.

“I’m getting me a Peanut Buster Parfait,” he announced, as if half the people there weren’t ordering the same. Cockiness oozed from his walk-and-talk like he was God’s gift to ice cream dispensers. But his entire demeanor changed when an “I gotta sneeze” facial grimace was soon joined by the inevitable “ah-ahh-ahhh.”

On vaporizing the word “chew,” the once cool dude in the DQ released the loudest, wettest sneeze humanity has ever produced while simultaneously thrusting his head forward, thwacking the wooden support beam in front of him. “Smack!” Great sneeze. Bad execution.

Past columns by the good doctor include "I Am Not a Robot" (“In addition to ‘not a robot,’ I wish to point out that I am also not a cheesy potato, though my wife and I differ on that one.”) Judging from the archives, his column was once called “Mud Puddles” but now it is not, or at least it is not tagged as such online.

I’m also a fan of this headline, from a different columnist.

I may have to start getting home delivery of the Winona Post.

Oldest living Racket co-owner and editor.

What went right this week: the good news that matters

Rewilding gave low-lying islands hope, a basic income trial showed promise, and a Bangladeshi factory won an award, plus more
The post What went right this week: the good news that matters appeared first on Positive News.

Actual Article Body:
Rewilding gave low-lying islands hope, a basic income trial showed promise, and a Bangladeshi factory won a global architecture award, plus more good news

Rewilding gave low-lying islands hope, a basic income trial showed promise, and a Bangladeshi factory won a global architecture award, plus more good news

Restoring seabird populations and native vegetation on low-lying tropical islands would give them a “fighting chance” against rising seas, a study has found.

Habitat loss and invasive rats wiped out seabirds on many tropical atolls. Now, scientists say that bringing them back could protect islands from rising seas after they discovered bird poo “supercharges” processes that help atolls grow.

“Islands are dynamic systems that shift and build over time,” said lead author Prof Nick Graham from Lancaster University, England. “Seabirds and native vegetation enhance geo-ecological functions that can help islands cope with sea level rise.”

Graham’s team found that coral reefs around islands with “thriving” seabird populations grew up to 2.5 times faster than those around rat-infested atolls. “Seabirds deposit large quantities of nutrients through their droppings, fertilising the reef,” he told Positive News, adding that reefs act as breakwaters during storms.

Production of sediment – the building blocks of tropical islands – was also significantly higher on seabird-rich atolls, allowing the islands to grow. Root systems of native plants, meanwhile, were shown to “hold islands together”.

The study, which examined 28 islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans, concluded that restoring native plants and seabirds on some atolls could help them “keep pace with even a 2C sea level rise projection”. Cutting emissions – and fast – is also crucial to their survival.

Related: The barren island that became a rewilding success

Image: Bruskov

Proponents of basic incomes have long argued that they could reduce inequality, improve health and boost the economy. Now, new research adds protecting the environment to the list of stated benefits.

Analysis of a two-year basic income trial in the Peruvian Amazon was published this week by the University of Bath, England. The pilot saw 211 people in three Indigenous communities receive cash transfers equivalent to around £2 a day to spend as they pleased.

Academics reported a sharp reduction in food insecurity – down from 73% to 26% – plus improvements to wellbeing. They also noted that many participants used the money to invest in education and solar, while 90% “adopted environmentally beneficial practices”, such as more sustainable farming practices.

“Giving historically marginalised Indigenous people a no-strings basic income brings a multitude of benefits,” said lead researcher Dr Neil Howard. “The incentive to exploit land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.”

The trial was small and there was no control group, but Cool Earth, the charity behind it, plans to expand the scheme. “Contrary to traditional critiques that basic income creates dependency or reduces work incentives, this pilot shows the opposite,” it said.

Related: The bold model stopping deforestation in its tracks

Image: Cool Earth

Combining exercise with volunteering could offer a “powerful” solution to the growing mental health crisis, researchers said this week.

Academics studied 2,800 volunteers at the UK charity GoodGym, whose members walk, run or cycle to help isolated older people and assist with community projects.

Regular participation was linked to a significant reduction in poor mental health compared to a control group, researchers found. Volunteers also reported improved feelings of trust, connectedness and belonging.

Mental ill health costs the UK alone an estimated £120bn annually through sick leave and productivity losses. Academics believe their findings provide policymakers with a cost-effective means of relieving pressure on stretched health services. Doctors in some UK regions already prescribe activities, such as walking in the woods, to improve patient health.

“Sports and volunteering can be powerful tools in addressing the growing mental health crisis documented in recent years and, in the context of increasingly stretched health resources, [are] highly cost-effective,” said Dr Maria Cotofan, senior lecturer in economics and policy at King’s College London, which led the research.

Image: AzmanJaka

He labeled the climate crisis a “hoax”, dubbed green energy a “scam” and re-entered the White House on a pledge to “drill, baby, drill” – yet US president Donald Trump is unwittingly presiding over a domestic clean energy boom.

Analysis from the Financial Times suggests that 2026 will be a bumper year for US renewables, with a record 45 gigawatts of clean-energy capacity forecast to come online. Meanwhile, green energy stocks have mostly outperformed their oil and gas rivals.

“The economics of green power are proving harder to overturn than the policies supporting it,” noted the newspaper. “Technological advances have made solar panels, wind turbines and batteries increasingly competitive, leaving renewables among the cheapest sources of new electricity generation in the US, even without subsidies.”

Trump’s war in Iran, which sent oil prices soaring, is one reason why renewables are taking off in the US. That’s not to say Trump’s policies aren’t stymieing climate action. A UN report warned this week that climate-warming pollution is soaring in the US, in contrast to other developed nations.

Image: WangAnQi

The Norwegian government has vowed to protect children from harmful content and addictive algorithms ahead of its anticipated under-16s social media ban.

Politicians are due to present a bill prohibiting children from using social media, one that is expected to make tech firms responsible for age verification.

In a statement on Monday, the government said the bill would address a range of risks children face online. “This includes everything from exposure to harmful content and addictive features to illegal marketing and unwanted contact from strangers,” said Lene Vaagslid, Norway’s children and families minister.

Norway has also announced a ban on “creepy” smart glasses. Under proposed legislation, camera-enabled spectacles will be prohibited in most public places, including parks and schools.

Since Australia became the first country to implement a social media ban for children, other nations have announced similar legislation, including the UK. Many children’s charities have welcomed such moves while others criticised them, claiming they are blunt instruments that punish children for tech company failures.

Image: Lacheev

A little-known landscape characterised by its towering rock spires has become the 64th US national park.

A 12,000-acre maze of rugged rock formations, Arizona’s Chiricahua landscape is a place where desert, grassland and forest ecosystems meet, supporting a remarkable array of biodiversity. On Tuesday, it became a national park.

“Chiricahua’s towering rock spires, rich Apache heritage and remarkable biodiversity make it one of America’s most extraordinary landscapes,” said secretary of the interior Doug Burgum. “This new designation will shine a national spotlight on one of Arizona’s hidden gems.”

The designation comes at a difficult time for US national parks. Since coming to power, the Trump administration has slashed the National Park Service’s budget and cut around 25% of its workforce.

Image: AZCat

A Bangladeshi rug factory has scooped a prestigious global award for “redefining manufacturing architecture in south Asia and beyond”.

Draped in plants and surrounded by gardens, Green Field rug factory in Rangpur is “more than just a place of work”, said judges at the RIBA International Prize.

The factory, commissioned by Karupannya Rangpur Ltd, uses nature to naturally cool the building. Workers inside have views of the surrounding landscape, plus access to a medical centre, daycare facility, prayer room and canteen.

“A factory should not be a machine that consumes human energy,” said Bayejid Mahbub Khondker of Nakshabid Architects, which designed the building. “It should be a living place that restores it. At Green Field, we wanted to prove that industry can breathe, nurture and inspire.”

Meanwhile, a housing development in London won RIBA’s Stirling Prize, awarded to the “UK’s best new building”. Lion Green Road contains 157 homes and is set in a verdant landscape in Croydon, London.

“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes, Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create,” said RIBA president Chris Williamson.

Image: City Syntax

If anywhere was going to blaze a trail in sustainable construction it was probably going to be a design museum.

Step forward Ghent, the forward-thinking Belgian city, which this week unveiled a new wing of its Design Museum, made largely out of recycled materials.

While its angular looks have divided aesthetes, the building’s commitment to the circular economy has been widely praised. As well as incorporating old sinks, toilets and windscreens, the building was constructed out of 85,000 bricks made from demolition waste.

Rather than being kiln-fired, the bricks were cured using hydrated lime. According to Carmody Groarke, the UK firm that led the design, this reduces embodied carbon by around two-thirds compared with conventional fired clay bricks. What’s more, “the lime binder continues to absorb carbon as it cures over time,” it added.

The new wing was part of a four-year renovation of the museum, which is now complete.

Image: Romanin & Noceto

Done well, solar farms have been shown to help boost biodiversity. Now, a new UK scheme aims to ensure more green energy sites benefit wildlife.

Launched by Wild Power, the scheme assesses how renewable energy developments protect and improve habitats, awarding certification to those that meet its biodiversity standards.

“I like to think of it as a fair trade stamp, but for clean energy,” Wild Power director Joe Arafa told Positive News. “Right now, we’re facing both climate and nature crises. A well-managed solar farm can contribute to solving both at the same time.”

Read the full story here.

Image: Hertha Wood, RES
Main image: helovi

Analysis of a two-year basic income trial in the Peruvian Amazon was published this week by the University of Bath, England. The pilot saw 211 people in three Indigenous communities receive cash transfers equivalent to around £2 a day to spend as they pleased.

Academics reported a sharp reduction in food insecurity – down from 73% to 26% – plus improvements to wellbeing. They also noted that many participants used the money to invest in education and solar, while 90% “adopted environmentally beneficial practices”, such as more sustainable farming practices.

“Giving historically marginalised Indigenous people a no-strings basic income brings a multitude of benefits,” said lead researcher Dr Neil Howard. “The incentive to exploit land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.”

The trial was small and there was no control group, but Cool Earth, the charity behind it, plans to expand the scheme. “Contrary to traditional critiques that basic income creates dependency or reduces work incentives, this pilot shows the opposite,” it said.

Combining exercise with volunteering could offer a “powerful” solution to the growing mental health crisis, researchers said this week.

Academics studied 2,800 volunteers at the UK charity GoodGym, whose members walk, run or cycle to help isolated older people and assist with community projects.

Regular participation was linked to a significant reduction in poor mental health compared to a control group, researchers found. Volunteers also reported improved feelings of trust, connectedness and belonging.

Mental ill health costs the UK alone an estimated £120bn annually through sick leave and productivity losses. Academics believe their findings provide policymakers with a cost-effective means of relieving pressure on stretched health services. Doctors in some UK regions already prescribe activities, such as walking in the woods, to improve patient health.

“Sports and volunteering can be powerful tools in addressing the growing mental health crisis documented in recent years and, in the context of increasingly stretched health resources, [are] highly cost-effective,” said Dr Maria Cotofan, senior lecturer in economics and policy at King’s College London, which led the research.

He labeled the climate crisis a “hoax”, dubbed green energy a “scam” and re-entered the White House on a pledge to “drill, baby, drill” – yet US president Donald Trump is unwittingly presiding over a domestic clean energy boom.

Analysis from the Financial Times suggests that 2026 will be a bumper year for US renewables, with a record 45 gigawatts of clean-energy capacity forecast to come online. Meanwhile, green energy stocks have mostly outperformed their oil and gas rivals.

“The economics of green power are proving harder to overturn than the policies supporting it,” noted the newspaper. “Technological advances have made solar panels, wind turbines and batteries increasingly competitive, leaving renewables among the cheapest sources of new electricity generation in the US, even without subsidies.”

Trump’s war in Iran, which sent oil prices soaring, is one reason why renewables are taking off in the US. That’s not to say Trump’s policies aren’t stymieing climate action. A UN report warned this week that climate-warming pollution is soaring in the US, in contrast to other developed nations.

The Norwegian government has vowed to protect children from harmful content and addictive algorithms ahead of its anticipated under-16s social media ban.

Politicians are due to present a bill prohibiting children from using social media, one that is expected to make tech firms responsible for age verification.

In a statement on Monday, the government said the bill would address a range of risks children face online. “This includes everything from exposure to harmful content and addictive features to illegal marketing and unwanted contact from strangers,” said Lene Vaagslid, Norway’s children and families minister.

Norway has also announced a ban on “creepy” smart glasses. Under proposed legislation, camera-enabled spectacles will be prohibited in most public places, including parks and schools.

Since Australia became the first country to implement a social media ban for children, other nations have announced similar legislation, including the UK. Many children’s charities have welcomed such moves while others criticised them, claiming they are blunt instruments that punish children for tech company failures.

A little-known landscape characterised by its towering rock spires has become the 64th US national park.

A 12,000-acre maze of rugged rock formations, Arizona’s Chiricahua landscape is a place where desert, grassland and forest ecosystems meet, supporting a remarkable array of biodiversity. On Tuesday, it became a national park.

“Chiricahua’s towering rock spires, rich Apache heritage and remarkable biodiversity make it one of America’s most extraordinary landscapes,” said secretary of the interior Doug Burgum. “This new designation will shine a national spotlight on one of Arizona’s hidden gems.”

The designation comes at a difficult time for US national parks. Since coming to power, the Trump administration has slashed the National Park Service’s budget and cut around 25% of its workforce.

A Bangladeshi rug factory has scooped a prestigious global award for “redefining manufacturing architecture in south Asia and beyond”.

Draped in plants and surrounded by gardens, Green Field rug factory in Rangpur is “more than just a place of work”, said judges at the RIBA International Prize.

The factory, commissioned by Karupannya Rangpur Ltd, uses nature to naturally cool the building. Workers inside have views of the surrounding landscape, plus access to a medical centre, daycare facility, prayer room and canteen.

“A factory should not be a machine that consumes human energy,” said Bayejid Mahbub Khondker of Nakshabid Architects, which designed the building. “It should be a living place that restores it. At Green Field, we wanted to prove that industry can breathe, nurture and inspire.”

Meanwhile, a housing development in London won RIBA’s Stirling Prize, awarded to the “UK’s best new building”. Lion Green Road contains 157 homes and is set in a verdant landscape in Croydon, London.

“At a time when we urgently need to deliver more homes, Lion Green Road shows that density can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create,” said RIBA president Chris Williamson.

If anywhere was going to blaze a trail in sustainable construction it was probably going to be a design museum.

Step forward Ghent, the forward-thinking Belgian city, which this week unveiled a new wing of its Design Museum, made largely out of recycled materials.

While its angular looks have divided aesthetes, the building’s commitment to the circular economy has been widely praised. As well as incorporating old sinks, toilets and windscreens, the building was constructed out of 85,000 bricks made from demolition waste.

Rather than being kiln-fired, the bricks were cured using hydrated lime. According to Carmody Groarke, the UK firm that led the design, this reduces embodied carbon by around two-thirds compared with conventional fired clay bricks. What’s more, “the lime binder continues to absorb carbon as it cures over time,” it added.

The new wing was part of a four-year renovation of the museum, which is now complete.

Done well, solar farms have been shown to help boost biodiversity. Now, a new UK scheme aims to ensure more green energy sites benefit wildlife.

Launched by Wild Power, the scheme assesses how renewable energy developments protect and improve habitats, awarding certification to those that meet its biodiversity standards.

“I like to think of it as a fair trade stamp, but for clean energy,” Wild Power director Joe Arafa told Positive News. “Right now, we’re facing both climate and nature crises. A well-managed solar farm can contribute to solving both at the same time.”
